messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Chung was a 35-year-old UX Designer with a South Eastern Asian background who had recently been struggling with intense psychological distress following his near-fatal battle with a serious illness. Married and devoted to his work, Chung’s trauma began when he faced life-threatening complications that left him feeling deeply vulnerable and afraid. Chung's traumatic experience led him to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person, an idea that only intensified his emotional numbness and sense of weakness. These negative appraisals made it difficult for him to engage in normal daily activities without feeling overwhelmed by fear and anxiety. He had come to avoid anything related to medical cues such as hospitals or ambulances and even physical examinations, which he found intensely distressing. Chung's belief that there was something inherently defective about himself led him to adopt maladaptive strategies like avoiding thoughts about the traumatic event entirely. He would distract himself with work tasks but often felt his body tense up in anticipation of potential danger. This constant state of alertness made it difficult for him to trust others when they assured him he was safe. Instead, delays in any situation—such as waiting for test results or even traffic delays—led him to assume the worst. As Chung’s negative appraisals deepened, so did his sense of threat and maladaptive coping mechanisms. He became hyper-vigilant about physical stressors at work, avoiding situations that might put his body under strain. His occupation as a UX Designer required long hours sitting in front of a computer, which he found increasingly stressful because he associated any discomfort with the possibility of another health crisis. The constant tension and heightened alertness also began to affect his relationships. Chung’s wife noticed him becoming more distant and withdrawn, often cancelling plans at the last minute out of fear that something bad would happen if they went out. This pattern of avoidance further reinforced his negative beliefs about himself, creating a vicious cycle where he was convinced his fears were justified. Chung had started to avoid medical appointments altogether, which made his wife even more concerned. He found it impossible to believe her reassurances and often felt that she didn’t understand the depth of his anxiety. His body remained on high alert, always ready for something bad to happen, no matter how irrational this seemed to others. The turning point came when Chung was unable to complete an important project at work due to a panic attack triggered by a minor delay in receiving necessary materials. This incident made him realize that his condition was affecting not just his personal life but also his professional success and reputation. He felt increasingly isolated, both from his colleagues and his family. Chung’s current state is one of intense fear and hopelessness. What frightened him most was the possibility of another health crisis without any control over it. Seeking help now seemed like a last resort to break this vicious cycle before it consumed him completely. While he hoped for relief from his constant anxiety, he also feared being seen as weak and vulnerable by those around him. The prospect of therapy felt daunting but necessary, a chance to reclaim some sense of normalcy in his life. Chung’s journey toward seeking help was marked by the realization that his fears and avoidance behaviors were not just symptoms but a cycle feeding on itself. He hoped for support and understanding from others so he could start to rebuild trust in himself and the world around him.
